name: Real Alcázar of Seville
label: Real Alcázar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza del Triunfo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza del Triunfo' (relation/5585601): middle (151 m across).
notes: Royal palace with Mudéjar architecture and gardens.

text.description:
The Real Alcázar is a royal palace in the heart of Seville, and it is still one of the official residences of the Spanish royal family. The site began as an Islamic-era citadel in the 10th century. After the Castilian conquest in 1248 it was rebuilt again and again, and the best-known part today is the richly decorated Mudéjar palace built by Pedro I in the 1360s. Together with the neighbouring Cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies, it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

For a phone photo, the outside is the easiest place to start. From the middle of Plaza del Triunfo you can step back far enough to fit the main gate, the Puerta del León, and the long brick walls into one frame, with the Cathedral and the Giralda close by. The square is open, so you have room to find the angle you want. Early morning is the time guides recommend, because the facade catches direct sun.

If you want a second picture, try Calle Agua, a narrow whitewashed lane with the palace wall on one side and bougainvillea overhead. The Jardines de Murillo also work well: palm and orange trees and tiled benches sit in front of the outer wall. The Patio de Banderas, just outside the palace exit, is free to enter and gives a good view of the Giralda, but it fills up with people leaving the palace.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Seville, right beside the Cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies. Plaza del Triunfo faces the Alcázar's main gate, the Puerta del León, across the open square.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Cathedral area in the centre of Seville. The Cathedral and Giralda are close to Plaza del Triunfo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the gate and walls in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is busy and you cannot step back any further. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the gate and the brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza del Triunfo (centre of the square, facing the Puerta del León). The Alcázar's main gate and brick walls framed across the open square, with the Cathedral and Giralda close by.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the gate up with the centre of the frame, keeping the walls straight and level. Step back until the whole entrance fits. For a different picture, try Calle Agua, where the whitewashed lane and bougainvillea lead the eye along the palace wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sunlit wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the brick keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the facade catches direct sun.

text.access_note: Plaza del Triunfo and the outside of the palace can be photographed from public space, but access to the palace itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Plaza de España
label: Plaza de España
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de España' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de España' (relation/4468922): middle (443 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Plaza de España, Seville'.
notes: Semicircular brick plaza with tiled alcoves and a canal.

text.description:
Plaza de España is a huge half-circle of brick and tile on the edge of Maria Luisa Park. It was built in 1928 for the Ibero-American Exposition of 1929 and designed by Aníbal González. It mixes Baroque, Renaissance and Moorish-inspired styles, which gives it plenty of detail for a phone camera. A canal curves in front of the building, and four bridges cross it, each standing for one of the ancient kingdoms of Spain. The Vicente Traver fountain sits in the centre, and the tiled alcoves along the walls each represent a different province of Spain.

The plaza photographs well because everything is symmetrical and curved. From the upper gallery balconies above the arcades, near the central section, you get a high, wide view with the canal, the central fountain and both towers in one frame. That extra height is why several guides rate it as the most iconic wide view of the square. Staircases at several points along the building lead up to the gallery. Back at ground level, the curved facade reflected in the canal makes a good second shot, and the sweep of the building leads the eye into the frame. The tiled alcoves are popular for portraits. The plaza has also appeared in films, including Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones. Water features are sometimes drained, which changes the canal shots, so be ready to focus on the architecture instead.
text.geographic_location: Plaza de España is in the southern part of central Seville, on the edge of Maria Luisa Park, which was the main site of the 1929 exposition.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot. The plaza is in Maria Luisa Park, in the south of Seville. Staircases along the building lead up to the gallery. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole curve of the plaza, the canal and both towers in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the central section. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the towers, the tilework and the alcoves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Plaza de España (upper gallery balconies above the arcades, near the central section). A high, wide overview of the whole plaza, with the canal, central fountain and both towers in one frame. The place to shoot from is the upper gallery balconies above the arcades, near the central section, which you reach by the staircases along the building. From the gallery, look out over the balustrade to see the canal, the central fountain and both towers together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the fountain with the middle of the frame so the symmetry looks deliberate. Keep the canal in the lower third and let the curve of the building run across the top. For a different shot, go back to ground level by the canal and bridge and photograph the semicircular facade with its reflection in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky and the brick keep their detail. Hold the phone level against the gridlines, because the curved lines show any tilt. Portrait mode works well for people in front of the tiled alcoves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning gives the emptiest frames, but one guide says the sun rises behind the main building, so much of the plaza stays in shade until late morning. Crowds build from about 10–11 AM, and the central bridges get busy then.

text.access_note: The plaza has been free to enter, but access is reported to be changing in 2026 and an entrance fee has been discussed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Seville Cathedral
label: Seville Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza del Triunfo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza del Triunfo' (relation/5585601): middle (151 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5641600: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathedral of Seville' (224 m across).
notes: The largest Gothic cathedral in the world.

text.description:
Seville Cathedral is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world, and it has a long story behind it. It was built on the site of a great mosque from the 12th century, the Almohad mosque, which had a minaret. The Giralda tower stands beside the cathedral. According to local tradition, the cathedral chapter decided in 1401 to build a church so grand that people would take them for mad. The Gothic building alone is 126 m long and 76 m wide, and the Giralda reaches 104.5 m to its weather vane. Work finished in 1506–7. It was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1987, together with the Alcázar and the General Archive of the Indies. Christopher Columbus is buried inside.

The cathedral is too big to fit into a frame from most places, which is the main challenge for a phone. Plaza del Triunfo gives you enough distance. From the far south-eastern corner you look north-west and see the whole south side of the building, with the Giralda rising above the roofline and the open square around it. Go early, ideally before about 9am, when the square is nearly empty and the south front is well lit. If you want a different view, Plaza Virgen de los Reyes shows the cathedral and the Giralda together. Patio de Banderas shows the tower at the end of a double row of orange trees, seen through an archway.

Take your time with the framing. Keep the phone level so the tall walls don't lean, and leave a little space above the tower.
text.geographic_location: Seville Cathedral is in Seville, Andalusia, Spain, beside the Alcázar and the General Archive of the Indies. The Archbishop's Palace is on its north-eastern side.
text.directions_text: Once you are there, the cathedral is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. Walk towards the cathedral walls and the Giralda tower, which you can see from far off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the south side with the Giralda above it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the building in the frame or the square is busy. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the Giralda and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza del Triunfo (far southeastern corner, shooting northwest toward the Giralda). The full south flank of the cathedral with the Giralda rising above the roofline, framed by the open square. From here the cathedral is to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the Giralda up with a vertical line so the tower stands straight. Leave some sky above it and some square below, so the building looks as big as it is. For a different version, try Plaza Virgen de los Reyes for the cathedral and tower together, or Patio de Banderas for the Giralda framed by orange trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. If you stay at 1x, take a second shot with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 9am, when the square is nearly empty and the south front is well lit.

text.access_note: The outside views from the squares are open public space and free, but entry to the cathedral and the Giralda may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Metropol Parasol
label: Metropol Parasol
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138602581: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Setas de Sevilla' (178 m across).
notes: Giant wooden mushroom-like structure with a rooftop walkway.

text.description:
Metropol Parasol, known in Seville as Las Setas or the Setas de Sevilla ("the Mushrooms"), is a huge wooden canopy over La Encarnación square in the old quarter. It was designed by the German architect Jürgen Mayer and finished in April 2011. It is roughly 150 by 70 metres and about 26 metres high. It is made of six parasols, shaped a little like giant mushrooms. Their form was inspired by the vaults of Seville Cathedral and by the ficus trees in the nearby Plaza de Cristo de Burgos.

It photographs well because the timber lattice makes strong curves and repeating patterns, and it sits against the older streets around it. Underneath are a market and a small museum of Roman and Moorish remains found on the site. The open-air plaza on the roof of the market level is shaded by the parasols, so you can stand right inside the structure and look up at the wood.

For your phone, make the structure the whole picture: look up, use the gridlines to keep the curves straight, and try a few frames from different spots under the canopy. A people-free shot is unlikely, so include a few figures to show the scale. The panoramic terraces on the upper levels give a view over the city centre, but check the official site before you go to see how access works.
text.geographic_location: On La Encarnación square, in the old quarter of Seville.
text.directions_text: Head for La Encarnación square in the old quarter of Seville. The spot has no listed nearby stations or tram stops. The phone icon on the map is at the middle of the structure, so once you are under the canopy you are there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of the parasols overhead, then switch to the default lens (1x) for tidier, less stretched frames. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the timber grid.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the plaza under the canopy and tilt the phone upwards to catch the curving wooden ribs.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up one of the main curves with a grid line so the lattice looks deliberate rather than tilted. Try one frame looking straight up for a symmetrical pattern, and another a little lower with a few people in it to show the size.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wood, not the sky, to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the bright sky stays blue. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a rail or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The low light of early or late in the day gives the wood a warmer colour. If it is lit after dark, night mode may help.

text.access_note: The plaza and market level are part of a public space, but the rooftop terrace and museum may be ticketed or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Low light early or late in the day gives the timber a warmer colour.

name: Casa de Pilatos
label: Casa de Pilatos
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Pilatos' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Pilatos' (way/116687580): middle (80 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2912100: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Casa de Pilatos' (116 m across).
notes: Andalusian palace mixing Mudéjar and Renaissance styles.

text.description:
Casa de Pilatos is a palace in Seville that is still the permanent home of the Dukes of Medinaceli. It mixes Italian Renaissance building with Mudéjar decoration, and it is often described as the model for the Andalusian palace. Building began in 1483. The name comes from the Holy Land pilgrimage of Fadrique Enríquez de Rivera, who completed the palace, and it has since been linked with the Way of the Cross in Seville. Inside, around 150 different tile designs from the 1530s make up one of the largest early tile collections in the world.

The free photo is outside, from the square in front of the entrance. Stand facing the main facade and tilt the phone upwards. The Renaissance marble gateway, designed in 1529 and topped with a Gothic crest, then stands out against the sky and trees. It is a good shot of the front on its own, and it gives you a record of the building before you go in.

If you do go inside, the main patio (fountain, marble columns, Mudéjar arches, tiled walls) and the small Jardín Chico garden are the other two places to photograph. Both are paid, so the square is the only spot that costs nothing.
text.geographic_location: Casa de Pilatos is in Seville, and the square in front of its entrance is the place to stand for the facade photo.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; use a map app to walk or get a taxi to Plaza de Pilatos. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is narrow and you want the whole facade and the sky above it. Otherwise use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the gateway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Pilatos (in front of the main facade, looking up at the building). The Renaissance front of the palace seen from the square, shot upward so the facade's curves stand out against sky and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Tilt the phone upwards so the curves of the Renaissance front stand out against the sky and trees. Use the gridlines to keep the facade from leaning too much, and leave a little space around the edges so you can crop later. Inside, the main patio and the Jardín Chico also photograph well, but they are paid and have their own photo rules.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Switch on the gridlines to keep the edges straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No set time is needed. Check how the light falls on the facade when you arrive, and try again in softer light if the sky is harsh.

text.access_note: The square in front of the entrance is free to stand in, but the palace itself is a ticketed interior site, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.

name: Santa Cruz
label: Barrio Santa Cruz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Santa Cruz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Santa Cruz' (way/67377793): middle (41 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4649140: large area 'Santa Cruz' (1858 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Medieval Jewish quarter with narrow whitewashed lanes.

text.description: Santa Cruz is the old Jewish quarter of Seville, a tight knot of whitewashed lanes, small squares and orange trees next to the Cathedral and the Real Alcázar. When Ferdinand III of Castile took the city, he gathered Seville's Jewish community into this one neighbourhood. After 1492 the area declined, and it was renewed in the 18th century. The best place to start with a phone is the Plaza de Santa Cruz. The square takes its name from a Mudéjar church that once stood here. It was pulled down during the Napoleonic Wars, and the old floor became the square. The painter Murillo was buried in that church. In the middle stands the wrought-iron Cruz de la Cerrajería, set in a small raised garden with steps, hedged paths and orange trees around it. That gives you a neat, layered picture: dark ironwork against pale walls, with greenery framing it. Guides describe it as a quiet, shaded spot. It is also pleasant in the morning, before the tour groups arrive. Take a wide shot of the whole square first, then step closer for the cross and the foliage. Keep an eye on the background, because people tend to wander through. Afterwards, wander the lanes towards the Cathedral side for narrow, shadowy street scenes where a vertical frame works well.
text.geographic_location: Santa Cruz is in the old centre of Seville, between the Jardines de Murillo, the Real Alcázar and Calle Mateos Gago, right beside the Cathedral and the Giralda. The Plaza de Santa Cruz is a small square inside the quarter.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground or tram stop right at this spot, so head for the Cathedral and Giralda area and walk into the quarter's lanes. The lanes are narrow and twisting, so use a map app to stay oriented. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the cross and its garden. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole square or the narrowest lanes, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the ironwork and orange-tree details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Santa Cruz (inside the raised central garden, on the paths beside the wrought-iron cross). The wrought-iron Cruz de la Cerrajería standing in the middle of the square, with orange trees and the surrounding hedged paths around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the cross on one of the vertical lines, with the hedges and orange trees filling the sides. Crouch slightly so the cross stands out against the pale walls behind it. The ultra-wide works well for the square, but keep the cross away from the edges, where it can stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cross to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls and bright sky stay detailed and the ironwork stays dark. In the shady lanes, hold the phone steady and let night mode help if the light is low.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive, is quieter. Soft light in the early morning or late afternoon is kinder than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The square appears to be an open public space, but check the official site before you go for any nearby ticketed sights such as the Cathedral or Real Alcázar.

name: Giralda
label: Giralda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Patio de Banderas' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Patio de Banderas' (way/22747262): middle (122 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/310065910: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'La Giralda' (22 m across).
notes: The former minaret turned bell tower of the cathedral.

text.description:
The Giralda is the bell tower of Seville Cathedral, and it began life as a minaret. It was commissioned in 1171 for the city's great mosque under the Almohad dynasty and finished on 10 March 1198, when four metal spheres were set on top. The Renaissance belfry was added later by the Christians. The main shaft is about 50 metres tall, with a smaller shaft above it. Inside, 35 ramps wind up around the core instead of stairs. The cathedral and the Giralda have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, together with the Alcázar and the General Archive of the Indies.

For a phone photo, the best-known angle is from Patio de Banderas. Stand at the far end, by the exit archway, and look back toward the cathedral side. The tower fills the arch at the end of a row of orange trees, which gives you a ready-made frame. Guides say it is also quieter than the cathedral square. If you want a different view, try Calle Mateos Gago, where the whole tower sits at the end of a tree-lined street. Plaza Virgen de los Reyes shows it from ground level in front of the cathedral, so you can see its four differently decorated faces. Early morning is the calmest time, and low sun lights the tower through the arch.
text.geographic_location: The Giralda stands beside Seville Cathedral in the old centre of Seville, close to the Alcázar. Patio de Banderas is the square reached from the Alcázar exit.
text.directions_text: Make for the cathedral and Alcázar area in the centre of Seville. Patio de Banderas is reached from the Alcázar exit. Once the Giralda is to the north-west, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the tower inside the archway. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more of the orange trees and the square. Try the telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the tower and its brick patterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Patio de Banderas (stand at the far end, looking back through the exit archway toward the cathedral side). The Giralda framed by the archway at the end of a row of orange trees. The Giralda is to the north-west and appears framed by the arch at the end of the row of orange trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the arch and let the tower fill the opening, with the orange trees leading toward it. Switch on the gridlines to keep the tower upright and the arch level. For variety, take a second shot from Calle Mateos Gago for the whole tower at the end of a street. From Plaza Virgen de los Reyes you can show the tower's different faces.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and pale stonework keep their detail. Because the archway is darker than the sky, take a couple of shots at different exposures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is quiet and low sun lights the tower through the arch.

text.access_note: Patio de Banderas is an open square, but it is reached from the Alcázar exit, so check the official site before you go for entry arrangements; the cathedral and tower may be ticketed, and guides say flash and tripods are not allowed inside the cathedral.
claims_not_in_sources: The Giralda stands in the old centre of Seville, close to the Alcázar.
A telephoto lens (2x or more) gives a tighter view of the tower and its brick patterns.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in the sky and pale stonework when shooting through the dark arch.
The archway is darker than the sky behind it, so bracketing a couple of exposures can help.

name: Hotel Alfonso XIII
label: Hotel Alfonso XIII
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Puerta de Jerez' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Puerta de Jerez' (node/8599790002): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/195567976: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hotel Alfonso XIII' (196 m across).
notes: Neo-Mudéjar luxury hotel built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition.

text.description: Hotel Alfonso XIII is a historic Neo-Mudéjar hotel in Seville. It was designed by José Espiau y Muñoz and built between 1916 and 1928 for the Ibero-American Exposition of 1929. It opened on 28 April 1929 with a banquet attended by King Alfonso XIII and Queen Victoria Eugenia. The style is Neo-Mudéjar, which here means Andalusian regional character built from fairly simple materials: mostly brick, plaster, wood and ceramics. On a phone screen that gives you warm red brick, pale detailing and decorative tilework in one frame. The hotel stands on Calle San Fernando next to the University of Seville, and the City of Seville owns it. The classic picture is the full front of the building seen across the square of Puerta de Jerez, directly opposite the main facade. From there you can get the whole frontage with some open space around it, which makes the photo feel balanced. Move in closer afterwards for the ceramic and brick details with the 2x or 3x telephoto setting if your phone has one. Turn on the gridlines so the vertical edges of the building stay straight, and hold the phone level rather than tilting it upwards. The hotel is a working luxury hotel, so photograph the outside from the public square and be discreet around the entrance.
text.geographic_location: Hotel Alfonso XIII is on Calle San Fernando in central Seville, next to the University of Seville and a short walk from the square of Puerta de Jerez.
text.directions_text: The hotel is east of the square, about 2 minutes on foot. Its main facade faces the square, so you can see where you are heading as you arrive. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). If the whole facade will not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the building in the middle of the frame so the edges are not stretched. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for brick and ceramic details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Puerta de Jerez (opposite the main facade, across the square). The full main facade of the hotel framed from the square, with its brick and ceramic Mudéjar-style detailing in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the main facade, switch on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them. Leave a little space above the roofline. For an alternative, walk to Calle San Fernando and shoot the main entrance straight on, with the hotel's name visible on the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the brick colour and ceramic detail are not washed out. Use Live Photos only if people are crossing the square and you want a lively moment to choose from.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on brick, with fewer harsh shadows. Check the facade is not in deep shade when you arrive.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the public square, but the hotel itself is a working hotel, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on brick facades.
From Puerta de Jerez the facade may be too wide for the default lens (1x), so the ultra-wide (0.5x) may help.
Building works or scaffolding could affect the view, so check the situation on the ground.
The hotel is open to guests as a working hotel, and visitors should be discreet around the entrance.

name: Torre del Oro
label: Torre del Oro
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Betis' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Betis nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28112279: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Torre del Oro' (22 m across).
notes: Twelve-sided riverside watchtower on the Guadalquivir.

text.description:
The Torre del Oro is a twelve-sided tower standing right on the edge of the Guadalquivir. It was built around 1220-21 under the Almohad governor of Seville to help control boat traffic on the river. It was once one of two anchor points for a great chain that could be stretched across the water. The name means 'Tower of Gold', and it is linked to the golden shine its building materials gave off on the river. The slim circular top level is a later addition, built in 1760 after the 1755 Lisbon earthquake damaged the original upper part. The people of Seville also objected when there was a plan to knock the tower down.

It photographs well because it is a simple, solid shape that stands apart from its surroundings, with open water in front. From the Triana bank you see the whole façade across the river, with its reflection and plenty of foreground. That is the classic postcard view. Guides also say the Triana side tends to be calmer than the city side.

For a phone photo, keep the tower upright and leave a little space above the top level and a little water below. If you want a different angle, try the middle of the Puente de Triana, which gives the tower on one side and the Triana waterfront on the other. Or try the Paseo Alcalde Marqués de Contadero for a low view with palm trees, river and sky.
text.geographic_location: The tower stands on the city bank of the Guadalquivir, at the edge of Seville's Arenal district. The Triana bank, where you take the photo, is directly across the water.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so make for the Triana bank of the Guadalquivir and Calle Betis on foot. The straight-line distance is about 3 minutes on foot, but the river is in between, so allow more time if you walk round by a bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which takes in the whole tower façade and the river in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more water and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the upper levels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Betis (Triana bank, directly opposite the tower). The whole tower façade, with its reflection in the river and the water in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Put the water in the lower third and the tower in the middle. Keep a little sky above the top level. For a different shot, try the Puente de Triana for the tower and the Triana waterfront together, or the Paseo Alcalde Marqués de Contadero for a low view with palm trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the tower's colour. Hold the phone steady for a sharp reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the low western light falls on the tower's river façade.

text.access_note: You can photograph the tower from the public street on the Triana bank, but if you want to go inside, check the official site before you go.

name: Triana
label: Triana
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle Betis' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Calle Betis nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4680655: large area 'Triana' (7047 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic riverside neighborhood known for ceramics and flamenco.

text.description: Triana is the neighbourhood on the western bank of the Guadalquivir, facing the old centre of Seville across the water. It has long been known for pottery and tiles, for flamenco and for its own festivals, and locals are proud of its separate character. For a phone photo, the best-known view is from Calle Betis, the street along the riverbank. The Calle Betis frontage is the postcard row of colourful Andalusian-style houses, and the river, the bridge and the Torre del Oro are in the view across the water. Guides single this out as the postcard view of Triana, and it works especially well in warm evening light and after dark, when the water picks up the lights. The Puente de Isabel II, the neighbourhood's best-known landmark, dates from the mid-19th century. At its western end stands a small Neo-Mudéjar chapel from 1927, and together they are the most recognised symbol of Triana. Calle Betis also has many restaurants and bars, so expect people strolling and sitting along the front. Take your first shot of the river and the view across it, then step in closer for details such as a doorway, a balcony or a tiled panel. If the pavement is busy, wait a moment for a gap rather than shooting over heads. Another good angle is from the bridge itself, which shows the riverfront and the Torre del Oro between the iron arches.
text.geographic_location: Triana is on the west bank of the Guadalquivir, across the river from Seville's historic centre, with Los Remedios to the south and La Cartuja to the north. The photo spot is on Calle Betis, the street that runs along its waterfront.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Seville, walk across the Puente de Isabel II to the Triana side of the river. Calle Betis runs along the water on the Triana side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the river and the bridge. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot step back. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for the Torre del Oro across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle Betis (Triana riverbank, the stretch facing the river). The row of colourful Andalusian-style buildings in the foreground, with the river, the Torre del Oro and the bridge across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the river on the lower third, keeping the phone level so the building fronts stay straight. For a second angle, try the Puente de Isabel II, which frames the Triana riverfront and the Torre del Oro in its iron arches. One guide also suggests Muelle de la Sal, from where you can photograph the houses of Calle Betis across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the lit facades to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against the railing or your body to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon for warm light on the houses, and after dark when the riverfront is lit.

text.access_note: Calle Betis is an open public street on the riverbank.
claims_not_in_sources: From the river stretch of Calle Betis, the Torre del Oro and bridge sit across the river, so you are looking towards the city bank.
The riverside pavement can be crowded in the evening, when you may need to wait for a clear gap.
Night mode benefits from keeping the phone steady against a railing or your body.

name: Parque de María Luisa
label: Parque María Luisa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de América' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de América' (way/40671555): middle (37 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/19394336: large area 'Maria Luisa Park' (1089 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large landscaped park with fountains and pavilions.

text.description:
Parque de María Luisa is Seville's main green space, a long public park beside the Guadalquivir. Much of it began as the gardens of the Palace of San Telmo, which the Infanta Luisa Fernanda gave to the city in 1893. From 1911 Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier reshaped it, and it then became one of the settings for the Ibero-American Exposition of 1929. That is why it is full of tiled fountains, ponds, pavilions and shady benches, with palms, orange trees and pines all around.

For a phone photo, the best-value spot is Plaza de América at the south end. Here the Mudéjar pavilion sits behind an ornamental pond, with the park's greenery around it. The square is often quieter than nearby Plaza de España, and its buildings give your pictures more depth than a shot of trees alone. The Cervantes monument, with its tiled scenes from his books, is close by. Doves gather in this part of the park, so a few birds in the foreground can bring a frame to life.

Once you have the wide view, walk north for the Bécquer monument. It and the Fountain of the Lions, elsewhere in the park, make good close-up subjects. Look for a tiled bench, a fountain or a pond edge to frame the scene, and keep your phone steady against a wall or railing for sharper shots.
text.geographic_location: The park lies in the south of Seville, stretching along the Guadalquivir, with Plaza de España on its edge. Plaza de América is at its southern end.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Plaza de España area at the edge of the park, by taxi or hired scooter if it is too far to walk. The centre of the park is north of there, about 6 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the pavilion, the pond and the trees into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for tile and carving details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de América (south end of the park, by the pond in front of the Mudéjar pavilion). The Mudéjar pavilion and its ornamental pond with the park's greenery around them, a wide view of the park's architecture. The park's centre lies to the north of this spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pavilion on one of the upper lines, with the pond filling the lower third. Use the pond edge or a tree branch as a frame. If you want a different view, the Glorieta de Bécquer shows the monument under its tall cypress, and the Isleta de los Pájaros shows a little island with its pavilion and the park's trees round the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the tiles and brickwork. Hold the phone at chest height to keep the horizon level. Take a Live Photo near the doves so you can pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and shadows under the trees. Midday sun can make shaded and sunlit patches too contrasty.

text.access_note: The park is a public green space, but pavilions, museums and other buildings inside may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Palace of the Countess of Lebrija
label: Lebrija Palace
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6378993: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo Palacio de Lebrija' (85 m across).
notes: Palace known for its Roman mosaic floors.

text.description: The Palace of the Countess of Lebrija is a house museum in central Seville. Its façade dates to the 16th century, and the house was remodelled between the 18th and 20th centuries. For a photographer it is worth visiting for the interiors. Moorish arches, Plateresque decoration, old tilework and a coffered ceiling sit side by side, and Roman mosaics pave almost the whole ground floor. The countess, Regla Manjón Mergelina, bought the palace in 1901 and filled it with antiquities from her archaeological interests. The best-known piece is the mosaic of the god Pan playing his flute to Galatea, in the central courtyard. The entrance hall has a floor of multi-coloured marble. The palace covers about 2,500 square metres over two floors, so there is plenty to frame, from wide courtyard views to close-ups of floor patterns, busts and tiles. The ground floor is open to wander at your own pace. The upper floor is visited on guided tours and its rooms are kept as the family lived in them. Start in the courtyard, where the mosaic, arches and surrounding rooms give you several compositions in one place. Then take close shots of single details: a tile panel, a carved column, a bust against a plain wall. Move slowly and wait for other visitors to step out of the frame. Rules on photography inside can differ by room, so ask staff if you are unsure.
text.geographic_location: The palace is in central Seville, Spain.
text.directions_text: Use a map app to find the Palacio de la Condesa de Lebrija in central Seville. The phone icon on the map is at the palace, so you can start shooting as soon as you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyard and larger rooms to fit in the arches and the floor. Use the default lens (1x) for most views. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for tiles, busts and small decorative details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Begin in the central courtyard, near the Pan mosaic, and turn slowly to see which arches and doorways frame well.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines so the arches and columns stay upright and the mosaic edges stay level. For the floor, hold the phone steady and point it down, keeping the lines of the pattern parallel to the edges of the screen. For details, step back a little and zoom rather than leaning in close.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of a room to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so lit areas do not wash out. In dim rooms, hold still and let night mode work if your phone offers it. Do not use flash near artworks.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the museum is quiet so you can photograph rooms without other visitors in the frame. Check the official site for visiting times.

text.access_note: This is a house museum, so entry rules, any ticket and the guided tours of the upper floor may apply; check the official site before you go, including whether photography is allowed.

name: Alamillo Bridge
label: Alamillo Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque del Alamillo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parque del Alamillo' (way/39729420): edge nearest the subject (1944 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/453809114: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Puente del Alamillo' (278 m across).
notes: Calatrava's cable-stayed bridge with a leaning pylon.

text.description:
The Alamillo Bridge is a single leaning white pylon with a fan of cables, and it is one of the most distinctive shapes on Seville's skyline. Santiago Calatrava designed it for Expo 92, and it was built between 1989 and 1992 to carry traffic across the Canal de Alfonso XIII to La Cartuja, the island where the Expo was held. The tower tilts backward and its weight alone balances a 200 m span, held by thirteen pairs of cables. There are no back cables behind it, which is why the bridge looks so bold and uncluttered. The deck also has a raised footway and cycle lane running between the traffic lanes.

It photographs well because the lines are so clean. The pylon, the cables and the deck make strong diagonals, and from the riverside path at the foot of the bridge you see the white tower rising above the trees, with the Guadalquivir in the foreground. Water and trees give you easy layers to build a picture around. Parque del Alamillo is the usual place to see the bridge from its base, so start there and walk along the path to try a few angles. For a more distant view of the pylon and cables, try the neighbouring Puente de la Barqueta. The viewing point at the top of the pylon is not open to the public, so don't plan a picture from up there. The bridge is lit at night, which gives you a second look after dark.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is on the edge of La Cartuja, the island in Seville that was the site of Expo 92, and it links the city side to the island. The park viewpoint is at its foot on the city side, beside the river path.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot. The park has a free car park at its entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole pylon, the deck and the river in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the cables against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque del Alamillo (riverside path at the foot of the bridge, on the city side). The white pylon and deck rising above the riverside trees, with the Guadalquivir in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the horizon level. Put the river or the path in the lower third and let the pylon rise through the upper part of the frame. Use the trees along the bank as a natural frame at the edges. For a different framing, the Puente de la Barqueta gives a more distant view of the pylon and cables.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white pylon to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white steel keeps its detail against the sky. Hold the phone upright, because tilting it back will make the tower lean even more. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides suggest sunset. The bridge is also lit at night, so it is worth coming back after dark for night-mode shots.

text.access_note: Parque del Alamillo is a public park with a riverside path, but check the official site before you go in case of any closures. The viewing point at the top of the pylon is not open to the public.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting the phone back makes upright structures appear to lean or converge, so holding it upright keeps the pylon straighter.
Exposing for the bright sky and white steel with the exposure slider helps to keep detail in the pylon.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) is wide enough to fit the whole bridge when standing close to its base.
Night mode works best with the phone held steady against something.

name: Puente de Isabel II
label: Puente de Isabel II
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Paseo Marqués de Contadero' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Paseo Alcalde Marqués del Contadero' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/236420470: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Puente de Isabel II' (180 m across).
notes: Iron bridge linking central Seville with Triana, also called Puente de Triana.

text.description:
The Puente de Isabel II, also called the Triana Bridge, is a metal arch bridge that links the city centre with the Triana neighbourhood across the Canal de Alfonso XIII, one of the arms of the River Guadalquivir. It was completed in 1852 and was the first solid bridge in Seville. Before it, people crossed on a pontoon bridge made of boats, first built by the Moors in the 12th century and kept going by repairs for around seven centuries.

It photographs well because the curved metal arches make a clear shape against the sky and the water. From the riverside promenade you see the whole bridge side-on, and the sun sets almost behind it at dusk. That gives you a dark outline, a glowing sky and reflections in the river. A second option is Calle Betis on the Triana bank, where the bridge sits in the frame across the water with the colourful riverfront houses lit warmly. A third is the Puente de San Telmo, for a zoomed view of the bridge with the Torre del Oro in front of it.

The promenade is a walkway, so people will pass through your frame. Wait a moment for a gap, or use them to give the picture a sense of scale. Keep the phone level, using the gridlines, so the bridge deck sits straight along the river.
text.geographic_location: The bridge spans the river in central Seville, joining the city-centre bank with Triana on the opposite side. The riverside promenade on the centre bank runs between the bridge and the Torre del Oro.
text.directions_text: Head for the Torre del Oro area on the city-centre bank of the river. From there, follow the riverside promenade (Paseo Marqués de Contadero) with the water beside you, heading north-west towards the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole bridge side-on. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand close and want the arches and the river together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) if you shoot from further along the river and want to bring the bridge closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Paseo Marqués de Contadero (riverside promenade on the city-centre bank, between the bridge and the Torre del Oro). The bridge seen side-on along the river, with the sun setting practically behind it at dusk.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge along the lower third, leaving room for the sky. Keep the river in the foreground so the arches reflect in it. For another view, walk over to Calle Betis on the Triana bank, where the bridge appears across the water with the Triana riverfront houses beside it. You can also zoom in from the Puente de San Telmo to get the bridge behind the Torre del Oro, but take care there, as the road is busy.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours stay rich and the bridge becomes a clean dark outline. After the sun has gone, try night mode and rest your elbows on something steady, or hold the phone against your body, to keep it sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the sun sets practically behind the bridge. Exactly where the sun goes and how busy it is varies with the season.

text.access_note: The bridge and the riverside promenade are public open-air spaces, so there is no ticket to think about; check the official site before you go if you plan anything beyond a walk by the river.

name: Plaza Nueva
label: Plaza Nueva
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Nueva' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Nueva' (relation/5617723): middle (194 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5617723: 'Fernando el Santo', the best-known feature inside 'Plaza Nueva' (194 m across).
notes: Central square facing the City Hall.

text.description:
Plaza Nueva is the open public square in front of Seville's city hall, and it is a good place for a simple, tidy photo. The long town hall facade, which dates from the 18th century, makes a calm backdrop. In front of it stands an equestrian statue of King Ferdinand III, who took Seville for the Christians in 1248 and was later declared a saint. The monument was inaugurated in August 1924. It is the natural foreground for your picture, and the wide, open paving gives you room to step back and fit everything in.

The square is younger than most in the centre. It was completed in 1856 on land that had belonged to a large convent from 1270 until 1840. Only one small chapel, San Onofre, survives from that convent. Locals have always called the place Plaza Nueva, even though it has had several official names over the years.

For the classic shot, stand on the open floor of the square and frame the statue with the town hall behind it. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines on your screen. The square also looks good after dark, when the town hall is lit up. If a tram happens to glide through, you may be able to catch it in the frame too. Temporary hoardings in the square may block some angles, so be ready to move a few steps.
text.geographic_location: Plaza Nueva is in the city centre of Seville, directly in front of the city hall (the Ayuntamiento). It sits on the site of the old San Francisco convent.
text.directions_text: Plaza Nueva is in the heart of central Seville and is easy to find on the map. From there the statue of Ferdinand III is about 40 m to the west, a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue and the town hall facade together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole open square and more sky. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the horse and rider.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Nueva (Open floor of the square, facing the Ayuntamiento (town hall) facade with the Ferdinand III statue in the foreground). The town hall's long facade framed by the equestrian statue of King Ferdinand III and the wide open paving of the square. The statue of Ferdinand III lies just to the west of you. Turn until the statue sits in the foreground with the long town hall facade spread out behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, with the facade running level across the frame. Crouch slightly so the horse and rider stand out against the building rather than the sky. If you want a second picture, try a tighter shot of the statue alone with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale sky and facade keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone still against your body or a firm ledge. Tap the lit facade to stop it burning out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light. After dark the lit-up town hall also makes a good picture.

text.access_note: Plaza Nueva is an open public square; for anything inside the town hall, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A tram runs through or arrives at Plaza Nueva and can be included in a photo.
Temporary hoardings or exhibition panels in the square may block some angles.
Early morning or late afternoon light is gentler for photography here.
The town hall facade is lit at night.

name: Basilica of La Macarena
label: Basílica Macarena
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Esperanza Macarena' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Nuestra Señora de la Salud y Esperanza' (way/1428123246): middle (69 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/40660624: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basílica de Santa María de la Esperanza Macarena' (62 m across).
notes: Home of the revered Virgin of Hope statue.

text.description:
The Basilica of La Macarena is a Catholic church in the Macarena neighbourhood, in the Old Town district of Seville. It is best known as the home of the Virgin of Hope of Macarena and the Jesús de la Sentencia sculptures, and it is the seat of the Brotherhood of the Macarena. The church is younger than many visitors expect. It was founded in 1941, designed by the Sevillan architect Aurelio Gómez Millán and finished in 1949. It was dedicated as a minor basilica in 1966. A museum about Seville's Holy Week opened here in 2009.

The church photographs well because of what stands around it. The Macarena Gate, one of the few remains of Seville's old walls, sits in front of the basilica, so old stone and a twentieth-century church can share one picture. Plaza de la Esperanza Macarena is described as being in front of the basilica entrance, so it is a separate spot, and you should check your location on the ground. Visitors also suggest the Arco de la Macarena, the yellow-and-white gate, as a second view, with the basilica's spire framed on the far side of the arch. Keep your phone upright for the gate and the spire, and turn it sideways for the long stretch of wall. Traffic and passers-by are part of the scene, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest.
text.geographic_location: In the Macarena neighbourhood of Seville's Old Town district, with the Macarena Gate, a surviving piece of the old city walls, in front of the basilica.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or station stops listed for this spot, so start from the Old Town and head north into the Macarena neighbourhood. Check your position on the ground before you start shooting. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wall and the building across the road. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the wall in the frame. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the basilica's spire through the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la Esperanza Macarena (in front of the basilica entrance; walk toward the main road and turn right). The old city wall alongside the road, and across the main road an old government building, both framed from the church forecourt area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone sideways and use the gridlines to keep the wall's top edge level. Let the wall run diagonally across the frame, with the building beyond it. As an alternative, walk to the Arco de la Macarena and frame the yellow-and-white gate around the basilica's spire. The wall beside the arch is fenced off, so shoot over or around the fence rather than trying to get past it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and the wall do not wash out. Use the ultra-wide lens only when you have room, as it can bend straight lines near the edges. Leave the flash off, and if you go inside, switch it off before you take any photos.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the wall and the gate than the middle of the day. This is a general suggestion, so check the light on the day.

text.access_note: The square and the wall are in public space, but the basilica is a place of worship with its own opening times, so check the official site before you go and avoid flash near the altar and during services.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.
Photography is generally allowed inside the basilica, but flash should be avoided near the altar and during services.
The wall beside the Arco de la Macarena is fenced off.
The Arco de la Macarena frames the basilica's spire on its far side.
The ultra-wide lens can bend straight lines near the frame edges.

The map's stand-here point is listed about 890 m north-east of the basilica outline, although Plaza de la Esperanza Macarena is described as in front of the basilica entrance; please verify the stand-here coordinates on the ground.

name: Hospital de la Caridad
label: Hospital de la Caridad
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2884360: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hospital de la Santa Caridad' (116 m across).
notes: Baroque church and charity hospital with Murillo paintings.

text.description:
The Hospital de la Caridad is a baroque charity hospital close to Seville's Real Maestranza bullring. It was founded in 1674 and still cares for older and frail people, so it is a working place as well as a sight. The hospital is dedicated to Our Lady of Charity, whose venerated 15th-century image is kept in the Church of Saint George of Lydda within the hospital grounds. The chapel is described as holding some of the city's richest baroque sculpture. Paintings by Murillo, made in 1668 for the brotherhood he belonged to, are part of its story. Four of the eight stayed in Seville, while the other four were taken in 1810 and now hang in galleries abroad.

It photographs well because of the contrast between a calm street frontage and a richly decorated interior. From outside, you will want the whole building in one frame, with straight vertical lines. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) if the street is narrow, but keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. The default lens (1x) gives a more natural view of the doorway and façade. If you go in, the telephoto (2x) is useful for carvings and gilded details without leaning over anything. Be discreet around the residents and any services, and check what the hospital allows before taking pictures inside.
text.geographic_location: In central Seville, near the Real Maestranza bullring.
text.directions_text: Make for the Plaza de toros de la Real Maestranza, as the hospital is close by. No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way is by taxi or hired scooter to the bullring, then continue on foot. Once there, follow the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the façade and doorway. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the building in, and to the telephoto (2x) for carved or painted details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For an exterior shot, step back to the street outside the hospital and look at the façade. If the chapel is open, take your interior pictures from just inside the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the walls up with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Keep the doorway central, then take a second, closer frame of a single detail. Indoors, hold the phone with both hands and keep your elbows tucked in to avoid blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone part of the wall to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop bright windows or sky washing out. Indoors, night mode can help in dim light, but hold still for the full capture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outside, an overcast sky or soft morning or late-afternoon light keeps the façade even. Inside, visit when the chapel is open and quiet.

text.access_note: The chapel is open to the public, but this is a working charity hospital and a place of worship, so dress respectfully and check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and photography rules.

name: Royal Tobacco Factory
label: Royal Tobacco Factory
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Calle San Fernando' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Calle San Fernando' (way/56767111): middle (405 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1020882: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Universidad de Sevilla - Rectorado' (287 m across).
notes: Grand 18th-century factory, now part of the University of Seville.

text.description:
The Royal Tobacco Factory (Real Fábrica de Tabacos) is a huge stone building from the 18th century. From 1758 until the 1950s it made snuff and cigars. Since the 1950s it has housed the rectorate of the University of Seville. When it was built it was the second largest building in Spain, behind only El Escorial. It still covers an area of about 185 by 147 metres. Building began in 1728 and production started in 1758. At its peak in the 1880s some 6,000 women worked here, and the fictional Carmen of Bizet's opera is a cigarrera from this factory.

It photographs well because the architecture is calm and well ordered. The stone façade is broken up by regular pilasters, and the arched entrance has a stone sculpture above it. Because the building is so large, the main task is fitting it into the frame. An alternative, from a different spot, is to cross to the far side of Calle San Fernando, face the main entrance (the Puerta de la Fama) and shoot straight on. This gives a symmetrical picture with the arch in the centre. Another quieter option is the side and western façade, seen rising above the dry ditch along the western side.

It is a working university building, so the outside is what you are here for. Keep to the pavement and do not step into the ditch. Check the official site before you go if you hope to see anything inside.
text.geographic_location: In central Seville, on Calle San Fernando, just outside where the old city gate, the Puerta de Jerez, once stood. The building is the seat of the University of Seville's rectorate.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Seville, head for Calle San Fernando, just outside the former Puerta de Jerez gate. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for the University of Seville rectorate (Real Fábrica de Tabacos). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole width in from the pavement. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the arch and the sculpture above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle San Fernando (across the street from the main entrance façade (Puerta de la Fama)). The full neoclassical main façade of the factory, with its arched entrance and the stone sculpture above it, shot straight on from the street. From here you can take in the stone, Renaissance-style building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the top and bottom edges of the building parallel to the grid, to stop the walls leaning. If you take the entrance view from across Calle San Fernando, line the entrance arch up with the centre line so the two halves of the façade match. For a less crowded alternative, walk round to the side and western façade, where the building rises above the dry ditch along the western side. Stay on the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. At 0.5x, keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where lines can stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No set time is needed. Choose a moment when the façade is lit rather than in shadow, and check how it looks on the spot.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but this is an active university building, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or take photographs for commercial use.

name: Plaza de América
label: Plaza de América
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de América' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2429567: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Park square with pavilions in María Luisa Park.

text.description: Plaza de América is a large, calm square inside the Parque de María Luisa in Seville. Three buildings, each in a different style, stand around the plaza, and a central pond sits in front of them. The most photographed view looks across the pond towards the Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions, a Mudéjar-style building whose facade is doubled in the water on a calm day. The plaza was designed by the architect Aníbal González for the Ibero-American exhibition of 1929. He also designed the three buildings around it: the Museum of Popular Arts (Neomudéjar), the Archaeological Museum (Neo-Renaissance) and the Royal Pavilion (Gothic). That mix of styles gives you plenty of variety without moving far. The plaza has also been used as a film location, including for an episode of The Crown. For the classic shot, stand at the central pond and face the Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions, keeping the water in the lower part of the frame. If you want something livelier, the southern end by the Glorieta de las Palomas has doves and people feeding them. The Glorieta de Cervantes has tiled benches and ceramics against the palms and greenery, which suits close-up details. Go early in the morning or in the late afternoon for fewer people and softer light on the tiles.
text.geographic_location: Plaza de América lies in the Parque de María Luisa, Seville, with the Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions, the Archaeological Museum and the Royal Pavilion around its edges.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Parque de María Luisa and walk to the plaza inside the park. Once there, the central pond is the best place to start. The phone icon on the map marks the plaza itself, so walk from it to the central pond. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pond and the museum facade together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole plaza, or to 2x or more to pick out the tilework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you see the Mudéjar-style facade reflected in the water, with the tiled buildings framing the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on a lower line so the reflection fills the bottom third. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. For a lively alternative, the Glorieta de las Palomas at the southern end gives you doves and people in the frame, and the Glorieta de Cervantes suits close shots of tiled benches.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright sky does not wash out the tiles. Wait for ripples to settle before you shoot, or try a Live Photo and pick the stillest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light warms the tiles; early morning is also quieter.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public space inside the Parque de María Luisa, but check the official site before you go for any changes to access, and for the museums if you plan to go inside.
